title: Review 2 | Connect administrative, clinical, and HIM systems
overview: This integrated review connects the administrative, clinical, and HIM systems considered in Weeks 8–11. Trace how one encounter or operational event is represented across connected systems, how its information is used, and where HIM controls support identity, meaning, quality, trust, and accountability.
objectives: Explain how healthcare organizations operate as ecosystems of connected systems, and how one event may generate clinical, administrative, coding, quality, and analytic data.
Use the Event → Systems → Data → Decision framework to explain information flow, responsibilities, and where control is needed.
Classify and compare systems by purpose, users, inputs, outputs, workflow, and controls.
Identify HIM responsibilities for protecting information identity, meaning, quality, privacy, security, trust, and accountability.

concepts.name: Data and meaning

concepts.name: Access and trust

concepts.name: HIM responsibilities
concepts.definition: HIM professionals explain system purpose, protect meaning and quality, support privacy and security, promote appropriate access and responsible disclosure, and improve workflows.

sections.body: Healthcare organizations operate as ecosystems of connected systems, not as isolated applications. One encounter or operational event can generate clinical, administrative, coding, quality, and analytic data. These outputs are not interchangeable: each system captures part of the event for a different purpose. For example, an emergency visit may produce registration, triage, laboratory, medication, discharge, coding, billing, and quality data. To explain the ecosystem, identify which system captures each part, what that system is for, and how the resulting information may be used. Administrative systems include finance, HRIS, MPI, scheduling, materials, facilities, and EIS. Clinical systems include CIS, CDS, DMS, RIS, LIS, nursing, pharmacy, and emergency. HIM functions include disclosure, encoder/grouper, registry, CDI, deficiencies, and quality indicators.
sections.title: Connected systems represent different parts of the same event

sections.body: Use the Event → Systems → Data → Decision framework to make information flow and control points explicit. First, identify the patient encounter or operational event. Next, identify the multiple systems that capture parts of it. Then consider how HIM validates identity, meaning, quality, and disclosure. Finally, identify how a person uses the information for care, operations, or reporting. The sequence helps distinguish the event itself from the systems that record it, the data those systems produce, and the decision made using that information. At each stage, ask who is responsible and where a control is needed.
sections.title: Trace information from event to decision

sections.body: A useful comparison begins with a system’s primary purpose: care, business, or HIM operations. Then identify its users, inputs, outputs, and workflow. Also name the output type: a record, transaction, recommendation, or report. These dimensions help explain how systems differ without treating their labels as sufficient descriptions. A complete account states the terms being compared, describes the difference, and gives a healthcare example. It also identifies controls that protect quality, privacy, security, and accountability.
sections.title: Classify systems by role, output, and control

sections.body: Reliable information depends on fit, meaning, trust, and usable workflow. Purpose and fit concern whether the system supports its intended users, work, outputs, and decisions; scope, workflow fit, and measurable objectives help assess this. Data and meaning concern whether information is complete, valid, consistent, timely, and understood; definitions, metadata, validation, and mapping support these qualities. Access and trust involve protecting privacy, security, integrity, and auditability through policy, role-based access, authentication, and logs. Workflow and adoption require that people can use information safely and effectively; user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement support that use.
sections.title: Apply quality, trust, and workflow controls

sections.body: HIM responsibilities span the information flow rather than stopping at a single system. HIM professionals explain a system’s users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits; support definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation; and check identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency. They also support privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure. To improve workflow, they use feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction. Together, these responsibilities help ensure information is fit for its intended use and that accountability is visible.

activities.title: Trace an emergency visit
activities.prompt: A hypothetical emergency visit generates registration, triage, laboratory, medication, discharge, coding, billing, and quality data. Which explanation best applies the Event → Systems → Data → Decision framework?
activities.debrief: The framework distinguishes the event from the multiple systems that capture it, the data and HIM validation involved, and the later use of information. The visit may generate data for different purposes.
options: Treat the visit as one system output, because the same event should produce only one kind of data.
Identify the visit as the event, trace which systems capture its different parts, consider HIM validation of identity, meaning, quality, and disclosure, and identify how people use the information.
Begin with the final decision and assume that all systems have the same purpose and controls.
Classify every output as clinical data because the event took place in an emergency setting.

activities.title: Recall the classification dimensions
